summary.text: A 22-year-old black man presented to the emergency department with 12 hours of periumbilical abdominal pain worsened by food, without nausea, emesis or a change in bowel habit, and reported childhood episodes of recurrent abdominal pain with occasional self-limited bowel obstruction. He had no relevant personal or family history, no fever or signs of peritonitis, normal vital signs and unremarkable blood tests.

Abdominal x-ray was non-specific with decreased bowel air content. Ultrasound showed a whirlpool sign of superior mesenteric vessel torsion with marked gastric distention and no free fluid, and acute midgut volvulus was diagnosed. Contrast CT showed the colon on the left, small bowel on the right and torsion and dilation of the superior mesenteric vessels. Urgent laparotomy confirmed midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation and a Ladd procedure was performed, followed by an uneventful post-operative course.

Two years after the Ladd procedure he was re-admitted with 48 hours of acute abdominal pain, without nausea, emesis or fever. The abdomen was distended, tympanic and tender with diminished bowel sounds, the white blood cell count was increased, and CT showed some free fluid, distended jejunal and ileal loops and a collapsed colon without an identifiable transition point, with no evidence of volvulus recurrence.

Because of tenderness, an elevated white blood cell count and free fluid on CT, a laparotomy was performed and a recurrence of the midgut volvulus around the mesenteric axis was found. After lysis of adhesions the bowel rotation was reduced and a colopexy of the cecum to the left gutter and a pexy in the right gutter were performed. The post-operative course was uneventful, and at 3 years of follow-up he had no other events or symptoms.
